title: NoodleClear
question: How are noodles made?
hook: A noodle is starch held in a net, pressed into a thread and set by heat. Pull one rope of dough into 4,096 strands, cook a strand from the outside in, then run an instant noodle line: steam, wave, and a minute in 150 °C oil that leaves every strand full of pores.

explainer.title: Starch in a net
explainer.text: Flour is mostly hard starch granules. In wheat noodles a stretchy net of gluten holds them. Kansui, an alkaline salt mix, makes ramen-type noodles yellow, firm and springy. Rice has no gluten, so idiyappam and sevai are set by steaming, and glass noodles are a clear gel of pure mung bean starch.

explainer.title: Cut, press or pull
explainer.text: Dough keeps its volume, so thinner means longer. Rollers take about 30% off a sheet at each pass before a slitter cuts it. A press pushes dough through a die, and the strands leave far faster than the piston moves. A lamian maker doubles the strands with every pull: twelve pulls give 4,096.

explainer.title: Cooking from the outside in
explainer.text: In boiling water, heat reaches the centre of a strand in seconds, but water takes minutes, and starch cannot gelatinise without it. Al dente is a thin core the water has not reached. A strand twice as thick takes about four times as long. Salt is for taste: 10 g a litre raises the boiling point by only 0.17 °C.

explainer.title: The instant noodle line
explainer.text: Strands fall onto a slower belt and buckle into waves, steam cooks the starch, and then about a minute in oil near 150 °C flashes the water to steam. Moisture drops from over 30% to a few per cent, pores are left behind, and oil fills some of them: a fried block is about 15 to 20% fat. Hot-air drying gives under 3% fat but fewer pores.

explainer.title: Why two minutes
explainer.text: The block was cooked at the factory, so hot water only has to get back in, and the pores are open doors. Fried blocks soften in roughly two and a half to four minutes, air-dried ones in four to six. A typical 70 g pack with its tastemaker is about 300 kcal, about 12 g of fat and well over half a day's sodium.

explainer.title: One idea, many noodles
explainer.text: Ask what it is made of and how the strand was formed, and you can place hakka noodles, udon, ramen, lamian, spaghetti, idiyappam, sevai, flat rice noodles, glass noodles and falooda sev on one map. India is now the third largest instant noodle market, at about 9.6 billion servings in 2025.

concepts.def: A tiny hard grain in which a plant stores starch. Wheat granules are up to about 55 micrometres across; rice granules are much smaller.
The stretchy protein net that forms when wheat flour is wetted and worked. It lets dough be rolled, cut and pulled.
Alkaline salts, sodium and potassium carbonate, that make ramen-type noodles yellow, firm and springy.
Starch granules absorbing hot water and swelling until their hard structure is lost. Wheat starch does it at about 51 to 60 °C.
Shaping dough by forcing it through the holes of a die, as in spaghetti, sev and idiyappam.
Cooked until only a thin, firm core is left in the middle of the strand.
A minute or two in oil at about 140 to 160 °C. Water boils out of the noodle and leaves pores behind.
Putting water back into a dried food. Pores make it fast.
Monosodium glutamate, a flavour enhancer in many seasoning sachets. Glutamate also occurs naturally in tomatoes, cheese and wheat.
